_**User (2026-10-21 23:27:22Z)**_

Enforce product ID when deleting a product variant #59

Context: This is an issue that was commented in the Medusa script but never resolved. In DELETE /admin/products/:id/variants/:variant_id (route.ts:66-91), it reads req.params.id but doesn’t actually use it to delete it. The workflow call is { ids: [variantId] /* product_id: productId */ }, where the product check is commented out, as well as the TODO comment, as well. Furthermore, the request to delete product variant B appears, but when it is actually called, the response returns product A as the parent, which is misleading.

User Scenario:
A user with admin privileges wants to delete a variant called variant_B, which is a component of product_B, but instead of calling the corresponding product it actually calls product_A in the URL by mistake. The user continues to delete the variant, but instead of showing the correct product, the response pulls product_A. As a result, the mistake goes missing, and the API would reject the request because the variant does not belong to that product.

Acceptance Criteria:

Deleting a variant that belongs to the product in the URL still succeeds/returns the same response
Deleting the variant under a product it doesn’t belong to returns an error (404 or 400) and it is not deleted.
Deleting a nonexistent product variant keeps its current status
The TODO commented out for product-id is removed
HTTP integration tests cover matching and mismatched cases.
Out of Scope:

Same check on variant endpoints unless they share the same code path (complete those separately)
Changes to variant creation or inventory handling
Bulk variant delete or batch endpoints
Admin dashboard UI changes

This is an issue I am going to start working on. Can you review the spec to make sure it is clear enough to implement and that it fits into the code?

import {
  deleteProductVariantsWorkflow,
  updateProductVariantsWorkflow,
} from "@medusajs/core-flows"
import {
  AuthenticatedMedusaRequest,
  MedusaResponse,
} from "@medusajs/framework/http"

import { AdditionalData, HttpTypes } from "@medusajs/framework/types"
import { refetchEntity } from "@medusajs/framework/http"
import {
  remapKeysForProduct,
  remapKeysForVariant,
  remapProductResponse,
  remapVariantResponse,
} from "../../../helpers"

export const GET = async (
  req: AuthenticatedMedusaRequest<HttpTypes.SelectParams>,
  res: MedusaResponse<HttpTypes.AdminProductVariantResponse>
) => {
  const productId = req.params.id
  const variantId = req.params.variant_id
  const variables = { id: variantId, product_id: productId }

  const variant = await refetchEntity({
    entity: "variant",
    idOrFilter: variables,
    scope: req.scope,
    fields: remapKeysForVariant(req.queryConfig.fields ?? []),
  })

  res.status(200).json({ variant: remapVariantResponse(variant) })
}

export const POST = async (
  req: AuthenticatedMedusaRequest<
    HttpTypes.AdminUpdateProductVariant & AdditionalData,
    HttpTypes.SelectParams
  >,
  res: MedusaResponse<HttpTypes.AdminProductResponse>
) => {
  const productId = req.params.id
  const variantId = req.params.variant_id
  const { additional_data, ...update } = req.validatedBody

  await updateProductVariantsWorkflow(req.scope).run({
    input: {
      selector: { id: variantId, product_id: productId },
      update: update,
      additional_data,
    },
  })

  const product = await refetchEntity({
    entity: "product",
    idOrFilter: productId,
    scope: req.scope,
    fields: remapKeysForProduct(req.queryConfig.fields ?? []),
  })

  res.status(200).json({ product: remapProductResponse(product) })
}

export const DELETE = async (
  req: AuthenticatedMedusaRequest<{}, HttpTypes.SelectParams>,
  res: MedusaResponse<HttpTypes.AdminProductVariantDeleteResponse>
) => {
  const productId = req.params.id
  const variantId = req.params.variant_id

  // TODO: I believe here we cannot even enforce the product ID based on the standard API we provide?
  await deleteProductVariantsWorkflow(req.scope).run({
    input: { ids: [variantId] /* product_id: productId */ },
  })

  const product = await refetchEntity({
    entity: "product",
    idOrFilter: productId,
    scope: req.scope,
    fields: remapKeysForProduct(req.queryConfig.fields ?? []),
  })

  res.status(200).json({
    id: variantId,
    object: "variant",
    deleted: true,
    parent: remapProductResponse(product),
  })
}

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-21 23:28:22Z)**_

The spec matches the code and is close to ready. One acceptance criterion contradicts the obvious fix, though, and a few smaller points need tightening before you start.

## What I confirmed in the code

- [route.ts:66-91](packages/medusa/src/api/admin/products/[id]/variants/[variant_id]/route.ts#L66-L91) is exactly as the issue says. `productId` is read, but only used to refetch the product for `parent`. The workflow gets `{ ids: [variantId] /* product_id: productId */ }`, and the TODO sits on line 73.
- `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow` only accepts `ids: string[]`. It has no product filter, so the TODO's worry is correct.
- That TODO appears nowhere else in `packages/medusa/src/api`, so nothing else shares this code path.
- GET and POST in the same file already pass `product_id: productId` into their lookups. That gives you the pattern to follow.

## Issues to fix in the spec

**1. "Deleting a nonexistent product variant keeps its current status" is ambiguous and probably conflicts with the fix.**
- **Current behaviour:** `softDeleteProductVariants` doesn't throw on unknown IDs. A nonexistent variant under a real product returns **200 `{ deleted: true }`**.
- **The conflict:** the natural fix is to look up the variant by `{ id: variantId, product_id: productId }` and throw `NOT_FOUND` when nothing comes back. That one lookup can't distinguish "variant doesn't exist" from "variant belongs to another product", so nonexistent variants would start returning 404 too.
- **Your options:** keep 200 for nonexistent variants (needs a second query, and keeps the misleading "deleted: true"), or accept 404 for both cases.
- **My recommendation:** accept 404 for both, and reword the criterion to: "Deleting a nonexistent variant returns 404."

**2. Pick 404 or 400.** "404 or 400" can't be tested. I'd choose **404 (`MedusaError.Types.NOT_FOUND`)**, since that's what GET/POST semantics imply. Then write the expected message into the criterion so the test can assert it.

**3. The user scenario mixes current and desired behaviour.** "The mistake goes missing, and the API would reject the request" describes both in one sentence. Split it:
- **Today:** variant_B is deleted, and the response shows product_A as `parent`.
- **Expected:** 404, and variant_B still exists.

**4. Say where the check goes.** You can either:
- **Check in the route (recommended):** query `variant` with `{ id, product_id }` and throw if it's missing, before the workflow runs. This is small, needs no change to `core-flows`, and matches GET/POST.
- **Add `product_id` to `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow`:** this changes a public workflow's API and its hooks, which is a bigger blast radius.

Adding "No changes to `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow`'s input" to Out of Scope would remove the guesswork.

**5. Reword the out-of-scope line.** "Unless they share the same code path" is fuzzy. Name it directly: "Only the DELETE handler in `[variant_id]/route.ts`."

## Things worth knowing (could be follow-up issues)

- **Nonexistent product:** if the product ID itself doesn't exist, the current DELETE ends with `refetchEntity` returning `undefined`, and `remapProductResponse(undefined)` should throw. That means a 500, though I haven't run it to confirm. The new check would turn this into a 404 for free, so it's worth adding as a test case.
- **GET and POST have the same weakness in a quieter form:**
  - A mismatched GET likely returns 200 with an empty `variant`.
  - A mismatched POST likely makes no change but still returns 200 with product A.

  Your spec rightly leaves these out, but each is worth its own issue.

## Tests

- **Where:** there is no dedicated `DELETE /admin/products/:id/variants/:variant_id` block today. The only delete call is incidental, in [product.spec.ts:2453](integration-tests/http/__tests__/product/admin/product.spec.ts#L2453). [variant.spec.ts](integration-tests/http/__tests__/product/admin/variant.spec.ts) is the natural home for a new `describe` block.
- **Cases:**
  - **Matching:** returns 200 with `parent.id === productId`.
  - **Mismatched:** returns 404, and a follow-up GET of the variant under its real product still returns it, which proves nothing was deleted.
  - **Nonexistent variant:** add this once you've settled issue 1.
  - **Optionally, nonexistent product:** returns 404.

If you make those wording changes, especially issues 1 and 2, the spec is ready to implement.

This plan assumes the teammate agrees to 404 for both the mismatched and the nonexistent cases. That way the whole change stays in one route handler and one test file.

## 1. Route change

**File:** [route.ts:66-91](packages/medusa/src/api/admin/products/[id]/variants/[variant_id]/route.ts#L66-L91)

Before the workflow runs, check that the variant exists under the product in the URL. [products/[id]/route.ts:41-55](packages/medusa/src/api/admin/products/[id]/route.ts#L41-L55) already does this with `refetchEntity` plus a `MedusaError`, so you can copy that pattern:

```typescript
export const DELETE = async (
  req: AuthenticatedMedusaRequest<{}, HttpTypes.SelectParams>,
  res: MedusaResponse<HttpTypes.AdminProductVariantDeleteResponse>
) => {
  const productId = req.params.id
  const variantId = req.params.variant_id

  const existingVariant = await refetchEntity({
    entity: "variant",
    idOrFilter: { id: variantId, product_id: productId },
    scope: req.scope,
    fields: ["id"],
  })

  if (!existingVariant) {
    throw new MedusaError(
      MedusaError.Types.NOT_FOUND,
      `Variant with id "${variantId}" not found for product "${productId}"`
    )
  }

  await deleteProductVariantsWorkflow(req.scope).run({
    input: { ids: [variantId] },
  })

  // refetch product + response unchanged
}
```

- **Imports:** add `MedusaError` from `@medusajs/framework/utils`.
- **Cleanup:** delete the TODO comment and the `/* product_id: productId */` fragment.
- **What it covers:** the one lookup handles all three error cases. A mismatched product, a nonexistent variant and a nonexistent product all return 404, and the 404 is thrown before anything is deleted.
- **What it leaves alone:** the workflow, the middleware and the response shape all stay the same.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-22 21:49:55Z)**_

Medusa's routing layer is where an HTTP request turns into business logic. Below is the full path of the request your change handles, `DELETE /admin/products/prod_A/variants/variant_B`.

## 1. The URL maps to a file (file-based routing)

Medusa doesn't keep a central route table. At startup, the framework's routes loader ([routes-loader.ts](packages/core/framework/src/http/routes-loader.ts)) walks `packages/medusa/src/api/` and turns each folder path into a URL:

```
api/admin/products/[id]/variants/[variant_id]/route.ts
     -> /admin/products/:id/variants/:variant_id
```

- Folders in square brackets, like `[id]`, become URL parameters, which the handler reads as `req.params.id`.
- Each HTTP method is a named export from `route.ts`: `GET`, `POST` and `DELETE`. Your file has all three, and each one is its own handler.

## 2. Middleware runs before the handler

Before your `DELETE` function runs, the request goes through several layers of middleware:

**a. Authentication (applied by the framework).** In [router.ts:495](packages/core/framework/src/http/router.ts#L495), the router automatically requires a logged-in admin `user` on everything under `/admin`. A request without a valid session or token gets a 401 here and never reaches your code. That's why route files never check auth themselves.

**b. Global middleware.** [api/middlewares.ts:84](packages/medusa/src/api/middlewares.ts#L84) adds cross-cutting concerns for all `/admin*` routes, such as `setSecretApiKeyContext`.

**c. Route-specific middleware.** [products/middlewares.ts:306-320](packages/medusa/src/api/admin/products/middlewares.ts#L306-L320) defines the entry for your route:

```typescript
{
  method: ["DELETE"],
  matcher: "/admin/products/:id/variants/:variant_id",
  middlewares: [
    validateAndTransformQuery(AdminGetProductParams, QueryConfig.retrieveProductQueryConfig),
  ],
  policies: [{ resource: Entities.product_variant, operation: PolicyOperation.delete }],
}
```

- **`validateAndTransformQuery`** checks the query string (for example `?fields=title,variants.*`) against a Zod schema. It then builds `req.queryConfig.fields`, falling back to the default admin product fields when the client doesn't ask for specific ones. That's why the DELETE handler can refetch the parent product with `req.queryConfig.fields`.
- **`policies`** is role-based access control. When RBAC is enabled, [router.ts:177](packages/core/framework/src/http/router.ts#L177) wraps the handler, so only admins allowed to *delete product variants* get through.

## 3. The handler: a thin orchestrator

By the time `DELETE` runs, the request is already authenticated, authorized and validated. The handler then does three things:

```
┌─ read params ─────── productId, variantId from req.params
├─ guard (your change) refetchEntity({ id, product_id }) -> throw NOT_FOUND
├─ mutate ──────────── deleteProductVariantsWorkflow(req.scope).run(...)
└─ respond ─────────── refetchEntity(product) -> res.json({ id, deleted, parent })
```

- **`req.scope`** is the dependency-injection container for this request. Everything the handler needs comes from it: module services, Query, workflows. Handlers never import a service directly.
- **Reads go through Query.** `refetchEntity` is a helper over Query (the remote query layer). Query can fetch data from any module and follow links between modules. Your guard uses it to ask the product module whether this variant exists with this `product_id`.
- **Writes go through workflows.** Routes don't call `productModule.softDeleteProductVariants()` directly. They run a workflow from `core-flows`. `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow` does much more than one service call:
  - removes the variant's links to other modules
  - deletes its inventory items
  - soft-deletes the variant
  - emits events

  Each of these steps has a compensation, so a failure partway through rolls back the earlier steps.
- **The response comes from a fresh read.** After the write, the handler queries the product again and returns it as `parent`. The client gets the current state, not whatever the workflow happened to return.

This split is why the check belongs in the route. The workflow takes only `ids` and is a public API that other code calls. The route is the one place that has both IDs from the URL, so it can enforce the "this variant belongs to this product" rule without changing the workflow's contract.

## 4. Errors become HTTP statuses in one place

When your guard throws `new MedusaError(MedusaError.Types.NOT_FOUND, ...)`, the handler never sets a status code. Express sends the error to the framework's error handler ([error-handler.ts:59-95](packages/core/framework/src/http/middlewares/error-handler.ts#L59-L95)), which maps error types to statuses:

| MedusaError type | HTTP status |
|---|---|
| `NOT_FOUND` | 404 |
| `INVALID_DATA`, `NOT_ALLOWED` | 400 |
| `UNAUTHORIZED` / `FORBIDDEN` | 401 / 403 |
| `DUPLICATE_ERROR` | 422 |
| `CONFLICT` | 409 |
| anything else | 500 |

The handler also sends your message to the client as `{ type, message }`, which is what the test checks with `response.data.message`. Because of this table, switching to 400 if your teammate prefers it is a one-word change from `NOT_FOUND` to `INVALID_DATA`.

## The full path at a glance

```
HTTP DELETE /admin/products/prod_A/variants/variant_B
  │
  ├─ router: /admin auth ............ 401 if not logged in
  ├─ global admin middlewares
  ├─ route middlewares: validate ?fields, build req.queryConfig
  ├─ RBAC policy check .............. 403 if not allowed
  │
  ├─ route.ts DELETE
  │    ├─ Query: variant {id, product_id} ── none? throw NOT_FOUND ─┐
  │    ├─ deleteProductVariantsWorkflow (links, inventory, delete, events)
  │    └─ Query: product -> res.json(...)                           │
  │                                                                 │
  └─ error handler <────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       NOT_FOUND -> 404 { type: "not_found", message: "Variant with id ..." }
```

The other routes in this repo follow the same pattern: validation and auth in middleware, a thin handler, reads through Query, writes through workflows, and errors mapped centrally. Files like `api/admin/orders/[id]/route.ts` are organized the same way.

_**User (2026-10-22 21:50:54Z)**_

Is this similar to a service layer?

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-22 21:51:08Z)**_

Yes, partly. The routing layer itself works like the **controller** layer in a classic layered architecture. The service layer still exists in Medusa, but it's split across two layers.

## Classic layers vs. Medusa

```
Classic                          Medusa
─────────────────────────        ─────────────────────────────────────────
Controller                  ->   API route (route.ts + middlewares.ts)
Service (business logic)    ->   Workflow (core-flows)       <- use cases
                                 Module service              <- one domain
Repository / DAO            ->   Repository + data models (MikroORM)
```

**Routes act as controllers.** They parse HTTP, validate input, call one piece of logic and shape the response. They hold almost no business rules.

**Module services are the domain service layer.** For example, `ProductModuleService` in `packages/modules/product` extends `MedusaService` and provides `softDeleteProductVariants`, `listProductVariants` and similar methods. Each module owns its own tables and **can't see other modules**. The product module knows nothing about inventory, pricing or sales channels. This isolation is the main way Medusa differs from a typical app, where one service can freely call another.

**Workflows are the application service layer.** Because modules are isolated, anything that spans modules has to be coordinated from above them. Deleting a variant is a good example: remove its cross-module links, delete its inventory items, soft-delete the variant, then emit events. That coordination is what `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow` does. In a classic app, a `VariantService.delete()` method would do this. Workflows add two things a plain service method doesn't have:
- **Compensation:** each step can undo itself, so a failure partway through rolls back the earlier steps without one database transaction spanning every module.
- **Hooks and reuse:** other workflows can run them as steps, and plugins can attach to their hooks.

## How this applies to your change

In a classic architecture, the "variant must belong to this product" rule would arguably sit in the service layer, not the controller. Medusa offers three places to put it:

1. **Route (what we did).** The check runs before the workflow. It's the smallest change and the workflow's public input stays the same. The downside is that the rule only protects this one endpoint.
2. **Workflow.** Add an optional `product_id` to `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow` and check it in a step. Every caller would get the protection, but it changes a public `core-flows` API. That's why we avoided it here.
3. **Module service.** This is effectively how GET and POST do it. They pass `{ id, product_id }` down as a filter, so the module only matches variants on that product. Delete-by-ID doesn't take a filter, so this option isn't available without changing the module's API.

Option 1 is the right size for this issue. If anyone asks in the PR review why the rule isn't in the service layer, the answer is that this is a deliberate trade-off. It also fits naturally in the design-decisions section, next to the route-level choice we already planned to note.

Written for: your team's PR reviewers.

This follows your template, plus the Design and Tech Debt sections from your format notes. I've added Tech Debt to those notes so future PRs include it too. The repo's `.github/workflows/action.yml` runs the HTTP integration tests on pull requests, so the CI line says to check that run. It doesn't say CI is missing.

---

## Summary

**What** — What changes are introduced in this PR?

`DELETE /admin/products/:id/variants/:variant_id` now checks that the variant belongs to the product in the URL before deleting it.

- A variant that belongs to a different product returns 404, and nothing is deleted.
- A variant that doesn't exist, or was already deleted, returns 404 (previously `200 { deleted: true }`).
- Deleting a variant under its own product works and responds exactly as before.
- The unresolved `TODO` and the commented-out `product_id` in the route are removed.

**Why** — Why are these changes relevant or necessary?

Closes #59

The route read the product ID from the URL but never used it to scope the delete. A request like `DELETE /admin/products/prod_A/variants/variant_B` deleted variant_B (which belongs to prod_B) and then returned prod_A as `parent`. That deleted the wrong data and hid the admin's mistake behind a misleading success response.

**How** — How have these changes been implemented?

- Before the workflow runs, the `DELETE` handler in `route.ts` looks up the variant with `refetchEntity({ id, product_id })`. If nothing matches, it throws `MedusaError.Types.NOT_FOUND`, and the framework's error handler turns that into a 404. GET and POST in the same file already scope by `product_id` the same way.
- `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow` is unchanged, and so is its public input.
- A changeset is included (patch).

**Testing** — How have these changes been tested, or how can the reviewer test the feature?

These tests were added to the existing `DELETE /admin/products/:id/variants/:variant_id` block in `integration-tests/http/__tests__/product/admin/variant.spec.ts`:

- **Matching product:** returns 200 with the same response shape (`id`, `object`, `deleted`, `parent`), and the variant is removed from `parent.variants`.
- **Mismatched product:** returns 404 with the error message, and the variant can still be fetched under its real product.
- **Nonexistent variant:** returns 404.
- **Already-deleted variant:** a second delete returns 404.

Results from a local run:

- All 15 product-related HTTP suites pass: 269 passed, 25 skipped (those were already marked `it.skip`).
- With the route change reverted, the mismatched test fails with `Expected: 404, Received: 200`, which reproduces the bug.

```bash
yarn workspace @medusajs/medusa build
cd integration-tests/http
npx jest __tests__/product/admin/variant.spec.ts -t "DELETE /admin/products/:id/variants/:variant_id"
```

---

## Examples

```ts
// variant_B belongs to prod_B
await sdk.admin.product.deleteVariant("prod_B", "variant_B")
// 200 { id: "variant_B", object: "variant", deleted: true, parent: { id: "prod_B", ... } }

await sdk.admin.product.deleteVariant("prod_A", "variant_B")
// 404 { type: "not_found", message: 'Variant with id "variant_B" not found for product "prod_A"' }
// variant_B is not deleted
```

---

## Design

**Decision:** Enforce the product/variant relationship in the route with a single `{ id, product_id }` lookup before calling the workflow.

**Alternatives considered:**
- Add an optional `product_id` to `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow`. Every caller would be protected, but it changes a public `core-flows` API.
- Use two lookups to keep the old `200` for nonexistent variants. That costs an extra query and keeps a misleading `deleted: true`.
- Return 400 for a mismatch instead of 404.

**Rationale:** This is the smallest change that fixes the bug. It matches how GET and POST in the same file already scope by product, and it doesn't touch the workflow other code depends on. Choosing 404 over 400 matches those handlers too.

**Consequences:**
- A nonexistent or already-deleted variant now returns 404, where it used to return 200. The issue's "keeps its current status" criterion was replaced with this, as agreed with the issue author.
- Each delete makes one extra read query.

**Other decisions:**
- **Error message** names both IDs (`Variant with id "X" not found for product "Y"`), so the admin can see which pairing was wrong.
- **Test scope** follows the spec's cases, plus the already-deleted case, because clients that retry a delete will hit it.

---

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:** The rule lives only in this route, not in `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow`. Other callers of the workflow, such as batch endpoints or custom code, aren't covered by this check. This was a deliberate choice, so that a public workflow API didn't change for this fix.

**Encountered:**
- **GET and POST on the same route:** they scope by `product_id` but likely return 200 on a mismatch (an empty variant or a no-op update) instead of 404. This is out of scope for #59 and left for a follow-up issue.
- **`softDeleteProductVariants`:** it silently ignores unknown IDs, which caused the old `deleted: true` for nonexistent variants. The route now guards against this; the service is unchanged.
- **`product.spec.ts`:** it has a skipped, commented-out legacy test for variant deletion ("TODO: Enable with http calls"). It was left as is; the new coverage is in `variant.spec.ts`.

---

## Checklist

- [x] I have added a **changeset** for this PR
- [x] The changes are covered by relevant **tests**
- [x] I have verified the code works as intended locally
- [x] I have linked the related issue(s) if applicable

---

## Additional Context

- **CI:** The repo's `.github/workflows/action.yml` runs unit tests and the HTTP integration tests on pull requests. Check that it passes on this PR before merging.
- **Limitations:** A nonexistent *product* in the URL now goes through the same lookup, so it should return 404 instead of the previous 500 from building the response. It has no dedicated test, to keep to the spec's scope. Admin dashboard callers already pass the correct product ID, so they're unaffected.

Mermaid is a good fit: you write the diagrams as text, check them against the code, and export the PNGs the assignment asks for.

## How to do it

**1. Write the diagrams as Mermaid source.** Keep the source files next to the images, so the diagrams can be reviewed and changed like code:

```
docs/sprint2/diagrams/
├── 59-njpiombino-class.mmd        # source
├── 59-njpiombino-class.png        # deliverable
├── 59-njpiombino-sequence.mmd
├── 59-njpiombino-sequence.png
└── 59-njpiombino.md               # template + Q&A
```

That folder doesn't exist yet, and I've assumed `njpiombino` as your username.

**2. Render to PNG.** Mermaid in this repo is only a library the docs website uses to draw diagrams. It isn't a tool you can run to make images, and this container has no browser for Mermaid's command-line renderer. The easiest options:
- **[mermaid.live](https://mermaid.live):** paste the source and use Actions, then PNG. Choose a large scale so the text stays readable.
- **VS Code:** the "Markdown Preview Mermaid Support" or "Mermaid Chart" extension shows a live preview while you edit.

**3. Mermaid can do everything the assignment grades:**

| Requirement | Class diagram | Sequence diagram |
|---|---|---|
| All relationship types | `*--` composition, `o--` aggregation, `-->` association, `..>` dependency, `<\|--` inheritance, `..\|>` realization | — |
| Existing vs. new | `classDef new fill:#fdf3dc,stroke:#c48a1e` and `class X:::new` | `rect rgb(...)` around the new steps |
| Annotations | `note for X "..."` | `Note right of X: ...` |
| Error path | — | `alt` / `else` blocks |
| Legend | a `note` or a "Legend" pseudo-class | a `Note over` block |

Mermaid places notes automatically, so you can't arrange them as freely as the amber boxes in the reference images. They are still notes on the diagram itself, which is what gets graded.

## What the diagrams should show for #59

**Class diagram.** Existing classes are drawn plain, and the new or modified parts are highlighted:
- **The route module** (`[variant_id]/route.ts`) with `GET`, `POST` and `DELETE`, where `DELETE` is *modified*. The annotation: the route is the only layer that has both IDs from the URL.
- **`refetchEntity`, a dependency over Query.** It's existing code, but the variant lookup by `{ id, product_id }` is *new*.
- **`deleteProductVariantsWorkflow`.** The annotation: its input is still `ids` only, and the workflow was deliberately left unchanged.
- **`ProductModuleService` and `softDeleteProductVariants`.** The annotation: unknown IDs are silently ignored, which was the root cause of the old `200 { deleted: true }`.
- **`Product` composed of `ProductVariant`** (`1 *-- 0..*`, through `product_id`). This is the relationship the fix enforces, so it's the obvious answer to Q&A question 2.
- **`MedusaError` (`NOT_FOUND`)**, a *new* dependency, plus the error handler that maps it to a 404.

**Sequence diagram:**
- An admin sends `DELETE /admin/products/:id/variants/:variant_id`.
- The router handles auth, query validation and the role check.
- The `DELETE` handler then calls `refetchEntity({ id, product_id })` through Query to the product module. That step is *new* and highlighted.
- `alt` **not found:** the handler throws `MedusaError(NOT_FOUND)`, the error handler turns it into a 404, and nothing is deleted.
- `else` **found:** the workflow runs `softDeleteProductVariants`, the handler refetches the product, and the response is 200 with `parent`.
- Annotations go on the guard ("runs before the workflow, so a mismatch deletes nothing") and the error mapping ("handler never sets a status").

The sequence diagram doesn't show auth failures (401) or role-check failures (403). That's the answer to Q&A question 3: those paths are existing behaviour and weren't changed.

## About the Q&A

Questions 1 to 3 ask for your own understanding, and question 4 asks how AI was used. If I draft the `.mmd` files, write down what you checked against the code and anything you corrected. That record is your answer to question 4.

I can draft the two `.mmd` files and the `.md` with the template filled in. You'd then render them on mermaid.live and write the Q&A answers.

Yes, the existing workflow can fail on its own. If the variant's inventory item has reservations, the workflow throws and rolls back the earlier steps. That's a good answer for one of the sequence questions.

Here are the confirmed facts for each question. Write your answers in your own words, and send me your drafts so I can check them against the code.

## Facts that are easy to misremember

| Topic | What's true |
|---|---|
| The old bug | The old code **did** delete the variant, then returned the *wrong* product as `parent`. The issue's "the API would reject the request" described the *desired* behaviour, not what happened. |
| Mismatch status | **404** (`NOT_FOUND`), not 400. You and your teammate agreed this. |
| Nonexistent variant | It **used to** return `200 { deleted: true }`, because `softDeleteProductVariants` silently ignores unknown IDs. It **now** returns 404. The spec's "keeps its current status" was replaced. |
| Already-deleted variant | A second delete now returns 404, because soft-deleted records aren't returned by Query. |
| What changed in code | Only the `DELETE` handler in `route.ts`: one lookup by `{ id, product_id }`, a thrown `MedusaError`, and removal of the TODO and the commented-out `product_id`. |
| What did *not* change | `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow`, `ProductModuleService`, the middleware, and the response shape on success. |
| Tests | 4 new tests in the **existing** `DELETE /admin/products/:id/variants/:variant_id` block in `variant.spec.ts`: matching, mismatched, nonexistent, already deleted. |
| Not tested | A nonexistent *product* in the URL. It should now return 404 (previously probably a 500), but nobody has run that case. |
| Error message | `Variant with id "X" not found for product "Y"`, naming both IDs. |

## Class diagram

**Q1. The most central classes.** Two strong choices:
- **The route module's `DELETE` handler.** It's the only place that has both IDs from the URL, and it's the only code you changed. It reads the params, runs the guard, calls the workflow, and builds the response.
- **`deleteProductVariantsWorkflow`.** Its input is `ids` only, which is *why* the check couldn't go there without changing a public API. Understanding this workflow explains where the fix had to live.

You could also choose `refetchEntity`/Query, since the guard is built on it. It's harder to argue that it's central to the *codebase* overall, though.

**Q2. The most significant relationship.** Two options:
- **`Product "1" *-- "0..*" ProductVariant`.** I'd pick this one. It's composition through `product_id`, and `Product` cascade-deletes its variants (confirmed in `product.ts`). The bug was that the route ignored this ownership link, and the fix enforces it.
- **`VariantRoute ..> refetchEntity`.** This dependency is new in your change, and it's how the guard actually checks ownership.

**Q3. What you'd change.** Pick what you actually believe. The real candidates:
- **The rule only protects this route.** Other code that calls `deleteProductVariantsWorkflow` directly isn't checked. Adding an optional `product_id` to the workflow would cover every caller, at the cost of changing a public API.
- **GET and POST on the same route** probably still return 200 on a mismatch (an empty variant, or an update that changes nothing). Fixing all three handlers together would make the route consistent.
- **Already-deleted variants now return 404**, so a client that retries a delete gets an error on the second try. You could argue for treating a repeat delete as success instead.
- **The guard adds one extra database read** per delete.

## Sequence diagram

**Q1. Trigger and outcome.**
- **Trigger:** an admin sends `DELETE /admin/products/:id/variants/:variant_id`. In the dashboard, that happens when deleting a variant from the product page or the variant page.
- **Successful outcome:** a 200 response with `id`, `object: "variant"`, `deleted: true`, and `parent` set to the variant's own product. The variant is soft-deleted, its links and any inventory items used only by it are removed, and a "variant deleted" event is emitted.

**Q2. The 2 or 3 most important steps.**
- **The guard lookup** (*new*): `refetchEntity("variant", { id, product_id })` through Query to the product module.
- **The throw on no match** (*new code*), turned into a 404 by the error handler (*existing*). The workflow never runs, so nothing is deleted.
- **The workflow run** (*existing*, apart from deleting the comment in the call): links are removed, inventory is cleaned up, and `softDeleteProductVariants` runs.

**Q3. Paths not shown.** These are all real cases, and all existing behaviour you didn't change:
- **401 and 403** from authentication and the role check, which happen before the handler runs. The diagram mentions this in a note.
- **400** when the `?fields` query string is invalid.
- **The workflow failing partway through.** For example, a variant whose inventory item has reservations makes `deleteInventoryItemWorkflow` throw "Cannot remove following inventory item(s) since they have reservations", and the earlier steps are rolled back. I confirmed that error and that path in the code. Your tests don't cover it.
- **A nonexistent product.** This goes through the same 404 branch as a mismatch, so it isn't a separate path.

The reason for leaving them out: they were already handled, your change didn't touch them, and showing them would bury the new branch.

## Cross-cutting

**Q4. How AI was used.** This is in my previous message: what was produced, what was checked against the code, and the one syntax fix. Add anything *you* checked or changed after rendering the diagrams, such as layout tweaks or wording.

When your drafts are ready, paste them here and I'll check every claim against the code.
